newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-Vienna to sell off Bank Austria.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Vienna to sell off Bank Austria.

text.p: Vienna launched Austria's biggest bank privatisation to date on Tuesday when the city's ruling coalition agreed to relinquish a 49 percent voting stake in market leader Bank Austria.

Analysts welcomed the move as a signal that politicians were finally withdrawing from the nation's banking sector but warned the sale could undermine Bank Austria's prestigious Aaa long-term credit rating, awarded on the basis of Vienna City guarantees.

Social Democrat mayor Michael Haeupl and his deputy Bernhard Goerg of the conservative People's Party presented the coalition proposal at a joint press conference. Vienna council was expected to rubber stamp the deal later on Tuesday.

"By the end of 1997 an international investment house will present a scheme for the sale,...taking into account the need to safeguard Austrian interests. A six-year timetable is foreseen," the proposal said.

"This is a significant challenge, perhaps the major challenge to face Austrian banking. But the fact they are selling sends a positive message," said James Alexander, banking analyst at Kleinwort Benson in London.

Vienna indirectly controls 45.15 percent of Bank Austria voting stock, or 39.93 percent of share capital, through its AVZ holding. A second firm, Wiener Holding, controls four percent of voting stock, representing 3.53 percent of capital.
The AVZ could, in theory, block the sale but Haeupl said he foresaw no problem in gaining the required two-thirds majority from AVZ's board, which is allied to the Social Democrats.
Goerg valued the AVZ stake at 25-35 billion schillings ($2.9 billion), dwarfing the 17 billion schillings raised for state coffers in January when Bank Austria bought rival Creditanstalt.
The People's Party had balked at that deal, which gave Social Democrat-dominated Bank Austria an unassailable position in the Austrian market.
"A complete privatisation of Bank Austria marks quite a big concession to the conservatives and tilts the balance of political power away from state ownership," an economist said.
The coalition parties agreed to seek buyers for the AVZ stake among institutional investors, strategic partners and via the stock market. The bank would remain under Austrian control.
"The privatisation must ensure that a majority Austrian interest remains and there is no significant decline in the share price," the motion said.

Once the sale was completed the City of Vienna would cease to act as guarantor for Bank Austria but Haeupl ruled out a deterioration in the bank's rating, insisting: "I don't believe there will be a negative impact."
Analysts disagreed, however. "I would expect the sale to have a negative bearing on Bank Austria's credit rating," said Alfred Reisenberger, an analyst at IMI Sigeco.
Moody's last month affirmed Bank Austria's Aaa long-term rating but awarded it only a C+ in terms of financial strength, which excludes the City of Vienna guarantee.
One Austrian banking source suggested that some clients may want to renegotiate deals struck on the basis of Bank Austria's Aaa rating.
Bank Austria preferred shares slipped 10.2 schillings to 435 in an otherwise stable Vienna market. ($ = 11.92 Austrian Schillings)
